sentences.text: Separate the heart wall from the sac around it.
The heart wall has three layers: epicardium outside, myocardium in the middle, and endocardium inside.
The myocardium provides most of the pumping force.
The endocardium lines the chambers and covers the valves.
The pericardium surrounds the heart.
Its serous layers and small amount of fluid reduce friction.
The visceral layer of serous pericardium is also the epicardium.
Most cardiomyocytes are working contractile cells; specialized cardiomyocytes initiate and conduct impulses.
They are striated, branched cells connected at intercalated discs.
Mechanical junctions help cells remain attached during contraction.
Gap junctions allow electrical current to pass between neighboring cells.
Together, these connections help groups of cells activate and contract in a coordinated way.
The heart has intrinsic electrical activity; nerves adjust its behavior rather than commanding every individual heartbeat.
Watch ventricular filling.
When ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure, the atrioventricular valves open and blood enters the ventricles.
Much filling is passive.
The slower middle portion of filling is called diastasis.
Near the end of ventricular diastole, atrial contraction adds more blood.
This contribution is sometimes called the atrial kick.
Its size varies with heart rate, age, and ventricular stiffness, so it is not a fixed percentage for every person or every beat.
Next, the ventricles begin to contract.
Rising pressure closes the atrioventricular valves.
For a brief period, the semilunar valves have not opened yet, so all four valves are closed.
Pressure rises while ventricular volume changes very little.
This is isovolumetric contraction.
The papillary muscles also contract, supporting the closed atrioventricular valves.
Remember the sequence: electrical activation starts first; force and pressure develop afterward.
When ventricular pressure exceeds pressure in the pulmonary trunk and aorta, the semilunar valves open.
Blood is ejected into the pulmonary and systemic circuits.
The atrioventricular valves remain closed during this phase.
The two ventricles work against different pressures, but they normally eject similar stroke volumes over time.
The heart does not empty completely with each beat; some blood remains in each ventricle after ejection.
As ventricular muscle relaxes, pressure falls and the semilunar valves close.
During isovolumetric relaxation, all valves are briefly closed again.
Once ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure, the atrioventricular valves reopen and filling resumes.
Systole refers to contraction; diastole to relaxation and filling.
These terms describe mechanical events.
An E C G is an electrical recording, so its waves are related to, but not identical with, these phases.
Heart rate is beats per minute.
Stroke volume is the volume ejected by one ventricle per beat.
Cardiac output is heart rate multiplied by stroke volume.
For example, seventy beats per minute times seventy milliliters per beat equals four thousand nine hundred milliliters per minute, or four point nine liters per minute.
A resting adult output around four to eight liters per minute is a broad teaching reference, not a result predicted from an E C G alone.
Stroke volume depends partly on preload, afterload, and contractility.
Preload relates to ventricular filling and muscle stretch before contraction.
Afterload is the load the ventricle must overcome to eject blood.
Contractility is the muscle's intrinsic ability to develop force.
Ejection fraction is stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume.
A commonly used left ventricular reference range is about fifty-five to seventy percent.
It is not the percentage of all blood in the body pumped per beat.
Check the pump before moving to electricity.
Which valves are open during ventricular ejection?
Which are open during most ventricular filling?
What happens to cardiac output if rate changes but stroke volume also changes?
Blood pressure reflects interactions among cardiac output, vascular resistance, and other factors.
A normal-looking rhythm does not prove normal pressure, normal ejection fraction, or adequate tissue perfusion.
